system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2177-10-19 22:22:00 to 2177-10-21 14:28:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for initiation of intravenous Remodulin therapy due to persistent hepatopulmonary syndrome despite prior treatment with sildenafil and inhaled treprostinil. A tunneled central venous catheter was successfully placed on 2177-09-01, and Remodulin was initiated at a low dose, gradually uptitrated to 5 ng/kg/min over 48 hours. He tolerated the therapy well with only mild fatigue, remained hemodynamically stable, and showed stable laboratory values. His home medications were continued, including management for cirrhosis, chronic pain from vertebral osteomyelitis, depression, and GERD. He was discharged home with a continuous Remodulin infusion, detailed education on pump and line care, and plans for outpatient dose adjustment to improve eligibility for liver transplantation.
problems: Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma

nodes are re- demonstrated compatible with prior granulomatous disease.  The
mediastinal and hilar contours are otherwise are unchanged.  Left-sided
central venous catheter has been removed.  No catheter fragments are
visualized, and no radio-opaque foreign bodies are seen.  The lungs are clear.
No pleural effusion, focal consolidation or pneumothorax is present.  There is
diffuse demineralization of the osseous structures.  Loss of height with
endplate scalloping of multiple thoracic vertebral bodies is relatively
unchanged compared to the prior chest CT from ___.

pneumothorax.  Little change in the appearance of the heart and lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. I understand your catheter came out tonight. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was doing my usual line care, and I noticed it was sticking out more than normal. Then when I wiped it, it just popped out and started bleeding a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I'm glad you came in right away. That’s the right thing to do. We’ve already placed a temporary IV and restarted your Remodulin through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried the medicine would stop. Does this mean I’ll need a new catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll need to replace it. It’s a tunneled catheter, just like before, but we’ll place it on the right side this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right side? Is that safe? I thought they always went on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s perfectly safe. We do it often. The right side works just as well, and it gives us a fresh site since the old one is no longer secure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will it be done tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, first thing in the morning. A specialist will place it using ultrasound and fluoroscopy to guide it into the correct spot in your vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tip goes into the big vein near the heart, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Into the superior vena cava. We’ll confirm the position with an X-ray afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I remember that from last time. Any risks I should know about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The main risks are bleeding, infection, or a punctured lung, but those are rare. We’ll monitor you closely after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been feeling okay otherwise. Just my usual back pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’re on several medications for pain from your osteomyelitis. Are they helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They help, but the Remodulin has made the pain a bit worse lately. Not sure why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some patients report that. We’ll keep your current pain meds going—gabapentin, morphine, and Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And I’ve had loose stools, so I’ve been skipping the Lactulose sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that. Remodulin can cause diarrhea. We’ll keep the Lactulose on board but adjust as needed to avoid making it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds—everything else stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications will continue—your diuretics, rifaximin, omeprazole, fluoxetine, and doxycycline for the osteomyelitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want anything changing unexpectedly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep things stable. Your labs look okay—your platelets are a bit low, but that’s expected with cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ve always been low. As long as I’m not bleeding, I’m okay with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And your liver numbers are stable. No signs of worsening cirrhosis or encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re getting ready to replace your catheter. You’ll go to interventional radiology in about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated—awake but relaxed. The team will numb the area and tunnel the catheter under the skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll get an X-ray after to check the position?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after. Fluoroscopy during the procedure will guide them, and a final chest X-ray will confirm it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The procedure went perfectly. Your new Hickman catheter is in place on the right chest, and the X-ray shows the tip is in the mid superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Is it safe to restart the Remodulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s already running. We connected it as soon as the line was secured. You’re back on your full dose—21.25 nanograms per kg per minute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any restrictions now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just keep the site dry and clean. We’ll teach you how to care for it before you go home. No heavy lifting for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your vitals are stable, and you’ve had no complications. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That was fast. Are all my meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no changes. You’ll continue all your home medications, including Remodulin, sildenafil, and your pain and liver meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And oxygen at night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2 liters at night as before. Your portopulmonary syndrome is stable, and we want to keep your oxygen levels up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your liver and pulmonary teams soon. They’ll manage your Remodulin and transplant evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep doing my part at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just watch the catheter site for redness, swelling, or fever, and call if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for getting this fixed so quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted after his Remodulin infusion catheter dislodged at home, causing minor bleeding. He presented to the emergency department where a temporary IV was placed and Remodulin was restarted. The tunneled catheter was successfully replaced on the right chest the following day without complications. Imaging confirmed proper catheter tip placement in the superior vena cava. His portopulmonary syndrome remained stable, and all home medications, including Remodulin, sildenafil, doxycycline, and pain regimens, were continued without change. He tolerated the procedure well, had no signs of infection or bleeding, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions for catheter care and follow-up with his specialty teams.
